To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the decision-making process of brown-headed cowbirds in response to oncoming vehicles was based on distance rather that time, and that cowbirds generally did initiate flight with enough to avoid collision when the vehicle speed exceeded 150 km h− 1.

1) cowbirds did not increase their alert and flight initiation distances as vehicle speed increased, 2) cowbirds did decrease their alert and flight times at faster vehicle speeds, 3) the decrease in alert and flight initiation time at faster vehicle speeds was not enough to allow the bird to avoid the oncoming vehicle, and 4) cowbirds did have enough time to initiate flight and avoid the oncoming vehicles when the speed of the vehicle was less than or equal to about 120

birds do not have enough time or distance to avoid vehicle collisions, and that they do not appear to be adjusting their escape behaviour as vehicles get faster, which is likely to result in high mortality.

how animals respond to vehicles and the factors that may contribute to their vulnerability to collisions.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the decision-making processes used by cowbirds are maladaptive in the face of fast-moving vehicles.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in the face of fast-moving vehicles, the ability to assess a potential threat and to make a quick decision may be more important than the speed of the escape response.
, as the speed of vehicles approaches or exceeds the flight speed of birds, birds are less able to assess the approaching threat and therefore less able to avoid it.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the speed of oncoming vehicles is a major factor in the ability of animals to avoid collisions.
, when faced with fast-moving vehicles, many animals may not have time to react and avoid collision.
, in order to reduce animal–vehicle collisions, it is critical to consider how the speed of vehicles affects animal escape responses and the time available for them to respond.
